# Root cause

The inconsistency is caused by `matplotlib.style.core.use()`'s private
`fix_style()` helper, and the fact that this aliasing/renaming logic is
applied **only** inside `use()` and never touches the `library` dict itself.

## What happens

In `lib/matplotlib/style/core.py`, `use()` defines a local function

```python
def fix_style(s):
    if isinstance(s, str):
        s = style_alias.get(s, s)
        if s in [
            "seaborn", "seaborn-bright", "seaborn-colorblind", ...
        ]:
            _api.warn_deprecated(...)   # the "renamed" deprecation warning
            s = s.replace("seaborn", "seaborn-v0_8")
    return s
```

and then does

```python
for style in map(fix_style, styles):
    ...
    elif style in library:
        _apply_style(library[style])
```

So when you call `plt.style.use('seaborn-colorblind')`, the name is first
silently rewritten (with a deprecation warning) to
`'seaborn-v0_8-colorblind'` *before* it is looked up in `library`. Since
`library` actually only contains the new `seaborn-v0_8-*` keys (populated
from the `stylelib` directory, which was renamed when the styles were
deprecated — see the list of names built in `core.py` and the corresponding
`.mplstyle` files under `lib/matplotlib/mpl-data/stylelib/`), the lookup
`library['seaborn-v0_8-colorblind']` succeeds and `use()` appears to work
fine for the old, deprecated name.

However, `library` (the module-level `_StyleLibrary`/dict returned by
`update_user_library`/`build_style_library`, exposed as
`matplotlib.style.library`) is populated directly from the on-disk
`stylelib` files and from `USER_LIBRARY_PATHS`; it is *never* updated with
the backward-compatible aliases. The alias/rename translation
(`seaborn-...` → `seaborn-v0_8-...`) lives exclusively inside `use()`'s
`fix_style` closure and is not shared with, or applied by, the `library`
mapping.

Consequently:

* `plt.style.use('seaborn-colorblind')` works, because `use()` internally
  rewrites the name to `'seaborn-v0_8-colorblind'` before indexing
  `library`.
* `plt.style.library['seaborn-colorblind']` raises `KeyError`, because
  `library` only ever contains the *new* names (`'seaborn-v0_8-colorblind'`,
  etc.) — the deprecated old-style aliases were never inserted into
  `library`, since the alias resolution logic exists only as a private,
  local helper (`fix_style`) inside the `use()` function and is not
  factored out into something that also updates/queries `library` itself.

## Summary

The bug/inconsistency is the fact that Matplotlib's "seaborn style rename"
backward-compatibility shim is implemented as string substitution local to
`style.core.use()` (the `fix_style` function), rather than as an actual
alias entry added to the `style.library` dictionary. This makes `use()`
transparently support the old `seaborn-*` names (with a deprecation
warning), while direct dictionary access via `style.library[...]` — which
does not go through `use()`/`fix_style` — does not recognize the old names
at all and raises `KeyError`.

results.answerText:
# Root cause

The inconsistency comes from `matplotlib/style/core.py`, specifically the
`use()` function, and the fact that the "old-name -> new-name" alias mapping
for the deprecated seaborn styles is implemented *only* inside `use()`, and
is never reflected in the `library` dict itself.

## What actually happens

1. `library` is a module-level dict built once at import time by
   `reload_library()` → `update_user_library(_base_library)` →
   `read_style_directory(BASE_LIBRARY_PATH)`.  This function just globs
   `*.mplstyle` files in `matplotlib/mpl-data/stylelib` and uses the file's
   stem as the dict key.  Since the seaborn style sheets were renamed on
   disk to `seaborn-v0_8-*.mplstyle` (e.g. `seaborn-v0_8-colorblind.mplstyle`),
   the *only* keys that end up in `library` are the new
   `"seaborn-v0_8-..."` names.  There is **no** entry for the old name
   `"seaborn-colorblind"` in `library` at all — so
   `plt.style.library['seaborn-colorblind']` unconditionally raises
   `KeyError`.

2. `plt.style.use(style)`, however, defines a **local, private** helper
   function `fix_style(s)` (defined inside `use()`, not exported or used
   anywhere else) that hard-codes a list of the old seaborn style names
   (`"seaborn"`, `"seaborn-bright"`, `"seaborn-colorblind"`, …). If the
   requested style string matches one of those old names, `fix_style`
   emits the "seaborn styles ... are deprecated" warning and rewrites the
   string by replacing the `"seaborn"` prefix with `"seaborn-v0_8"`
   (e.g. `"seaborn-colorblind"` → `"seaborn-v0_8-colorblind"`). Only *after*
   this rewriting does `use()` look the name up in `library` (`elif style in
   library: _apply_style(library[style])`). Because the rewritten name does
   exist in `library`, `use('seaborn-colorblind')` succeeds and prints the
   deprecation warning.

## The inconsistency

`fix_style()`/the alias table and the associated deprecation warning are
private implementation details tucked away inside the `use()` function.
They are applied only when a style name flows through `use()`.  Any other
consumer of the public `library` mapping — e.g. directly indexing
`plt.style.library[...]`, or iterating `plt.style.available` — bypasses this
alias-resolution step entirely, since `library`/`available` are built solely
from the on-disk `.mplstyle` file names and never had the old
`"seaborn-*"` aliases added to them (nor is `fix_style` called when building
them).

This is really a design bug: the renaming/backward-compatibility mapping for
the deprecated seaborn style names was added only in the single call site
`use()`, instead of being applied uniformly wherever style names are
resolved (in particular, it should have also populated `library`/`available`
with the deprecated aliases, or the KeyError-triggering resolution logic in
`use()` should be factored into a shared helper used by both `use()` and
direct `library` access). Because of this, `plt.style.use('seaborn-colorblind')`
"succeeds silently" (after a warning) while `plt.style.library['seaborn-colorblind']`
and similarly `'seaborn-colorblind' in plt.style.available` fail with a
`KeyError`/`False`, even though both are supposed to represent the same style
namespace.

results.finishSummary: The bug is in Media.merge() in django/forms/widgets.py: it does a naive pairwise, position-based merge of only two lists at a time (with a single reused insertion cursor) rather than building a full precedence/dependency graph from all lists and topologically sorting it, so merging is not associative—accidental orderings introduced by earlier two-list merges cause false MediaOrderConflictWarnings and a final JS order that violates FancyTextWidget's own explicit, non-conflicting ordering.
results.answerText:
# Which function is responsible

The combination of JS (and CSS) lists is done by `Media.merge()` (a static
method on `django.forms.widgets.Media`, in `django/forms/widgets.py`). It is
called repeatedly by the `Media._js` property (and `_css`) to fold each
widget/form's media list into a single, cumulative "js" list, one pairwise
merge at a time:

```python
@property
def _js(self):
    js = self._js_lists[0]
    for obj in filter(None, self._js_lists[1:]):
        js = self.merge(js, obj)
    return js
```

For the example in the question, the three widgets contribute the JS lists

```
['color-picker.js']                                            # ColorPicker
['text-editor.js']                                              # SimpleTextWidget
['text-editor.js', 'text-editor-extras.js', 'color-picker.js']  # FancyTextWidget
```

and `_js` calls `merge()` twice:

```
merge(['color-picker.js'], ['text-editor.js'])
merge(<result>, ['text-editor.js', 'text-editor-extras.js', 'color-picker.js'])
```

# What is wrong with `merge()`'s approach

`merge(list_1, list_2)` only ever looks at **two lists at a time** and tries
to interleave them by walking `list_2` in reverse and inserting/repositioning
items into a copy of `list_1`, using a single `last_insert_index` cursor. This
algorithm has two related problems:

1. **It has no real "ordering constraint" model** – it does not derive a set
   of pairwise precedence constraints ("A must come before B") from each
   input list and then find an order consistent with the union of those
   constraints (as a proper topological sort would). Instead it does an
   ad-hoc positional insert/merge of exactly two sequences, which is
   equivalent to a two-way "diff/patch" style merge, not a true multi-list
   merge.

2. **Because there's no accumulated constraint graph, merging is not
   associative** — merging `list_1` and `list_2` and later merging that result
   with `list_3` can scramble ordering information that was implicit in
   `list_1`/`list_2` but is not literally present as adjacent items in the
   partial merge. In the example:
   - `merge(['color-picker.js'], ['text-editor.js'])` produces
     `['text-editor.js', 'color-picker.js']` (a perfectly reasonable partial
     order, since neither original list said anything about the relative
     order of `text-editor.js` vs `color-picker.js`).
   - When this two-element list is then merged with FancyTextWidget's
     `['text-editor.js', 'text-editor-extras.js', 'color-picker.js']`, the
     algorithm walks the *new* list in reverse and, upon meeting
     `color-picker.js`, finds it already in `combined_list` at an index
     *before* `last_insert_index` was set from `text-editor-extras.js`
     insertion — but only because `color-picker.js` had previously been
     placed *before* `text-editor.js` in step 1 (an ordering that
     FancyTextWidget never actually requested and that came from an
     essentially arbitrary earlier merge decision, not a true constraint).
     The algorithm therefore concludes there is a conflict between
     `text-editor-extras.js` and `text-editor.js`, even though every one of
     FancyTextWidget's *own* declarations keeps them in the same relative
     order (`text-editor.js` before `text-editor-extras.js` before
     `color-picker.js`) in all three input lists that mention them.
   - The final combined list Django produces
     (`['text-editor-extras.js', 'color-picker.js', 'text-editor.js']`)
     actually violates FancyTextWidget's stated order (which requires
     `text-editor.js` before `text-editor-extras.js` before
     `color-picker.js`), while at the same time (incorrectly) warning about a
     conflict that doesn't exist between `text-editor.js` and
     `text-editor-extras.js`.

In short: `Media.merge()` performs a naive, position-based, pairwise
list-splicing merge (with a single "insertion cursor" reused across a
reversed walk) instead of building a proper dependency/precedence graph from
*all* the lists being combined and topologically sorting it. Because it only
ever compares two lists at once, and mutates a running "combined" list whose
internal relative ordering was itself the accidental byproduct of an earlier,
unrelated pairwise merge, it (a) raises false-positive
`MediaOrderConflictWarning`s for orderings that no single input list actually
required, and (b) can produce a final ordering that contradicts the explicit,
non-conflicting ordering declared by one of the inputs (here,
`FancyTextWidget.Media.js`).

results.finishSummary: Media.merge (django/forms/widgets.py) is the culprit: it does a greedy single-cursor pairwise merge instead of a real topological sort, so it both raises a false MediaOrderConflictWarning and produces a combined JS order that violates FancyTextWidget's declared ordering; full explanation written to ANSWER.md.
results.answerText:
# Which function is responsible?

`django.forms.widgets.Media.merge` (a `@staticmethod` in `django/forms/widgets.py`,
around line 118). It is invoked by the `Media._js` (and `Media._css`) properties,
which fold the list of per-widget JS lists together by repeatedly calling
`Media.merge(accumulated, next_widget_js)`.

For the example in the question, the widget media are combined pairwise, in the
order the widgets are declared/merged:

1. `merge(['color-picker.js'], ['text-editor.js'])`
   → `['text-editor.js', 'color-picker.js']`
2. `merge(['text-editor.js', 'color-picker.js'],
         ['text-editor.js', 'text-editor-extras.js', 'color-picker.js'])`
   → this call is where the incorrect warning and incorrect result are produced:
   `['text-editor-extras.js', 'color-picker.js', 'text-editor.js']`

That final order puts `text-editor.js` *after* `color-picker.js` and after
`text-editor-extras.js`, which violates the ordering explicitly required by
`FancyTextWidget.Media.js = ['text-editor.js', 'text-editor-extras.js',
'color-picker.js']`. It also spuriously warns that `text-editor-extras.js` and
`text-editor.js` conflict, even though both source lists always place
`text-editor.js` before `text-editor-extras.js` — there is no real conflict at all.

# What exactly is wrong with `Media.merge`'s approach

`merge(list_1, list_2)` implements a heuristic, one-pass, "insert-as-you-go"
algorithm rather than a real topological sort of the partial orders implied by
the two lists:

```python
combined_list = list(list_1)
last_insert_index = len(list_1)
for path in reversed(list_2):
    try:
        index = combined_list.index(path)
    except ValueError:
        combined_list.insert(last_insert_index, path)
    else:
        if index > last_insert_index:
            warnings.warn(...)  # "opposite order"
        last_insert_index = index
return combined_list
```

Problems with this approach:

1. **It only tracks a single "last_insert_index" cursor**, not the actual
   position/precedence relationships of every element pairwise. As soon as an
   element from `list_2` is found already present in `combined_list`,
   `last_insert_index` is forcibly reset to that element's index — regardless of
   where later (previously processed, since we iterate in reverse) elements from
   `list_2` were placed. This means the algorithm can move elements from
   `list_2` to a position that is *before* other elements of `list_2` that were
   already merged in, even though `list_2` requires them to come *after*.

   Concretely: walking `['text-editor.js', 'text-editor-extras.js',
   'color-picker.js']` in reverse gives `color-picker.js`,
   `text-editor-extras.js`, `text-editor.js`. `color-picker.js` is found in
   `combined_list` at index 1, setting `last_insert_index = 1`.
   `text-editor-extras.js` is new, so it gets inserted at index 1 — i.e.
   *before* `color-picker.js*, which is fine on its own — but then
   `last_insert_index` becomes 1 (the new position of `text-editor-extras.js`).
   Finally `text-editor.js` is found already in the list at index 0, which is
   **less than** `last_insert_index` (1), yet the code raises a warning anyway
   for the *wrong reason* (it interprets "index != last position it expected"
   as a genuine ordering conflict) and then forces `last_insert_index = 0`,
   which now sits *after* the newly-inserted `text-editor-extras.js`/
   `color-picker.js` block in effect, scrambling the final order to
   `['text-editor-extras.js', 'color-picker.js', 'text-editor.js']`.

2. **The algorithm is order-of-merge dependent and non-associative.** Because
   it is a greedy, single-pass, pairwise merge rather than a proper
   topological sort over the union of ordering constraints from *all* lists,
   the final combined order (and even whether a warning fires) depends on the
   arbitrary order in which the individual widget media lists happen to be
   folded together (e.g., `merge(merge(A, B), C)` can give a different, and
   here incorrect, result compared to directly computing a consistent
   linearization of the constraints "text-editor.js before
   text-editor-extras.js before color-picker.js" together with "color-picker.js"
   and "text-editor.js" as singletons).

3. **The warning heuristic is unsound.** It fires whenever, during the
   reversed walk of `list_2`, an element already present in `combined_list` is
   found at an index greater than the previously recorded `last_insert_index`.
   This condition does not actually correspond to "these two elements appear in
   conflicting relative order in `list_1` and `list_2`" — it is an artifact of
   the single-cursor bookkeeping, so it produces false positives (as shown
   here: `text-editor.js` and `text-editor-extras.js` are in the *same*
   relative order in every input list, yet a `MediaOrderConflictWarning` is
   raised claiming otherwise) and it does not detect all *real* conflicts
   reliably either, since it depends on merge order and can miss/misattribute
   conflicts depending on which list is `list_1` vs `list_2` and the sequence
   of merges performed by `Media._js`/`Media._css`.

In short, `Media.merge` conflates "keep relative order stable when possible"
with a fragile positional heuristic instead of performing a correct
topological sort of the ordering constraints declared across all the merged
lists. That is why it both raises a bogus conflict warning for
`text-editor-extras.js`/`text-editor.js` (which never conflict) and produces a
final combined order that violates the only real constraint declared by
`FancyTextWidget.Media.js`.
